messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus Webb

Marcus Webb was thirty-two when he first felt the tightness in his chest. He'd gone to the emergency room on a Tuesday evening, certain he was having a heart attack—the pressure radiating through his ribs, the shortness of breath that wouldn't ease even when he sat down. The diagnosis came back: acute myocarditis, inflammation of the heart muscle, likely viral in origin. For three weeks he was admitted to the cardiac unit, hooked to monitors, subjected to echocardiograms and stress tests, needles threaded into his forearms for blood draws and IV lines. The doctors assured him he'd recover fully with rest and medication. He did recover, physically. But something else had taken root during those nights listening to the beep of monitors, watching nurses approach with syringes, feeling his heart skip and stutter beneath the electrode pads.

Five years later, Marcus sits in his apartment in Portland, a database administrator for a mid-sized tech firm, and he cannot remember the last time he felt truly safe in his own body. The illness itself is long resolved—his cardiologist has cleared him repeatedly—yet the fear has metastasized into something larger, something that now governs how he moves through the world. He had come to believe that his body was fundamentally unreliable, a vessel that could betray him without warning. This conviction sits beneath everything he does, a constant low-frequency hum of dread. When he feels even the slightest flutter in his chest, or a moment of shallow breathing, the old panic rises: *it's happening again, you're dying, your body is failing you.* The certainty is absolute and immediate, and it drives everything that follows.

Because of this constant threat, Marcus has constructed an elaborate architecture of control. He monitors his eating with obsessive precision, restricting his caloric intake and avoiding foods he believes might stress his heart—salt, sugar, anything that makes him feel heavy or sluggish. The act of refusing food, of saying no to his body's hunger, gives him a temporary sense of mastery. If he can control what goes in, perhaps he can prevent catastrophe. He has stopped exercising entirely, despite knowing intellectually that his cardiologist recommended gentle activity. But the thought of elevating his heart rate, of feeling it pound in his chest, is intolerable. He tells himself that rest is safer, that movement invites danger. He avoids hospitals, refuses routine physical exams, and has not seen his primary care physician in three years. When his company scheduled a health screening last fall, he called in sick. The thought of sitting in a medical office, of having a blood pressure cuff around his arm or a stethoscope on his chest, triggered such acute panic that he could not bring himself to attend.

Yet these strategies, meant to protect him, have become their own source of threat. His restricted eating has left him feeling weak and depleted; his avoidance of exercise has deconditioned his body, making even climbing stairs leave him breathless—which then confirms his fear that something is wrong. The avoidance itself generates new moments of panic. Last month, a colleague mentioned chest pain during a meeting, and Marcus felt his own chest tighten in sympathetic dread. His body responded as though the danger were his own: muscles rigid, breath shallow, a wave of hot shame that he could not control his reaction. He has noticed, too, that the more he avoids medical situations, the more catastrophic they seem in his imagination. He has begun to experience his body as constantly on alert, perpetually braced for the next crisis. His shoulders are chronically tense, his sleep is fragmented, and he startles at unexpected sounds. He finds himself scanning his body for symptoms throughout the day—*is my heart rate elevated? Do I feel dizzy? What was that sensation in my left arm?*—a vigilance that exhausts him but which he cannot seem to stop.

His divorce two years ago coincided with a period of particular isolation; his ex-wife had grown weary of his health anxiety, and he had pushed away friends who suggested he see a therapist. Now, at thirty-seven, he works from home most days, a choice that began as practical but has become a refuge. He avoids the office, avoids chance encounters with colleagues, avoids the unpredictability of the outside world. The isolation has deepened his rumination. What finally brought him to seek help was a panic attack so severe that he convinced himself he was having a stroke—the fear was so real, so physically overwhelming, that he sat on his bathroom floor for two hours unable to move. In the days after, something shifted. He realized that the illness he survived five years ago had not killed him, but the fear of it might yet destroy his life. He is terrified that therapy will require him to face medical situations, to feel his heart race without fleeing. But he is also, for the first time, wondering whether the control he has built is actually keeping him safe, or whether it has simply become another prison.
